One Nation, One Allegiance: The Case for Banning Dual Citizenship

An Argument for Singular National Loyalty

The concept of citizenship is among the most sacred bonds in political life. It represents a covenant between the individual and the state—a mutual commitment of protection, loyalty, and shared destiny. In the United States, this covenant has historically demanded what the Oath of Allegiance plainly states: that one "absolutely and entirely renounce and abjure all allegiance and fidelity to any foreign prince, potentate, state, or sovereignty." Yet despite this unambiguous language, the United States has drifted into a permissive tolerance of dual citizenship that undermines the very foundations of republican self-government. It is time to restore the principle that American citizenship demands undivided allegiance by banning dual citizenship for all who claim the privileges of being American.

The Historical Foundation of Singular Allegiance

The Founders of the American republic understood, with a clarity that has since been obscured, that divided loyalty is a threat to the integrity of democratic governance. The Constitutional Convention debated at length the dangers of foreign influence, and the resulting document reflects a pervasive concern with ensuring that those who govern and participate in American civic life owe their fidelity to no other sovereign. The requirement that the President be a natural-born citizen, that members of Congress meet lengthy residency requirements, and that naturalized citizens formally renounce prior allegiances were not arbitrary formalities—they were structural safeguards against the corrosion of divided loyalty.

For most of American history, the law reflected this understanding. The Bancroft Treaties of the late nineteenth century established agreements with numerous nations stipulating that naturalization in one country constituted renunciation of citizenship in the other. The Expatriation Act of 1907 explicitly stripped American women of their citizenship upon marriage to a foreign national, a provision that, while rightly criticized for its gender discrimination, reflected the prevailing and arguably correct principle that a person cannot serve two sovereign masters. This principle was not unique to the United States; it was recognized across the international community as fundamental to the coherent functioning of nation-states.

The erosion of this principle began in earnest with the Supreme Court's 1967 decision in Afroyim v. Rusk, which held that the Fourteenth Amendment prevents the government from involuntarily stripping citizenship from an American. While the decision was defensible on narrow constitutional grounds regarding involuntary expatriation, its practical consequence was to open the floodgates to dual citizenship by removing the government's ability to enforce the logical implications of acquiring foreign nationality. This judicial shift was never accompanied by a democratic deliberation about whether the American people wished to abandon the principle of exclusive allegiance. The result has been a de facto policy of toleration that serves neither the nation nor, ultimately, the dual citizens themselves.

The Problem of Divided Loyalty

The most fundamental argument against dual citizenship is the simplest: genuine allegiance cannot be divided. Citizenship is not a consumer product to be accumulated like frequent flyer memberships. It is a profound political relationship that carries obligations—the obligation to defend the nation, to serve on juries, to participate honestly in self-governance, and to prioritize the common good of one's political community. When a citizen holds simultaneous allegiance to two nations, these obligations inevitably come into conflict, and the result is that at least one allegiance becomes hollow.

Consider the most elemental obligation of citizenship: the duty to defend one's country in time of war. If the United States were to enter into armed conflict with a nation whose citizenship an American also holds, that individual faces an impossible moral and legal dilemma. Whose flag does he fight under? Whose cause does he support? The standard response from proponents of dual citizenship—that such conflicts are rare and that individuals can navigate them with personal judgment—is dangerously naive. The entire architecture of national defense depends on the certainty that citizens will answer the call of their nation without reservation. Introducing ambiguity into this most fundamental obligation is not a mark of cosmopolitan sophistication; it is a structural vulnerability.

Beyond the dramatic scenario of armed conflict, divided allegiance creates countless quieter but equally corrosive problems. A dual citizen serving in the United States Congress may be called upon to vote on trade agreements, sanctions, military aid, or diplomatic policies affecting the other country of their citizenship. Can the American people be fully confident that such a representative's judgment is unclouded by competing loyalties? The question is not whether any particular individual would act improperly—it is whether the system should tolerate a structural conflict of interest at the very heart of democratic representation. In virtually every other context, American law recognizes that conflicts of interest must be eliminated, not merely managed. A judge must recuse himself from cases involving personal interests. A corporate director cannot simultaneously serve on the boards of competing companies. Yet we tolerate the far graver conflict of simultaneous allegiance to competing sovereigns in the most consequential arena of all: national governance.

The problem extends into the realm of national security with particular urgency. Dual citizens may hold security clearances, serve in sensitive government positions, or access classified information while maintaining legal obligations and emotional attachments to foreign governments. Intelligence agencies have long recognized that divided national loyalties represent one of the most significant vectors for espionage and information compromise. This is not speculation—the history of espionage is replete with cases in which individuals exploited their access to serve the interests of another nation to which they felt bound. Banning dual citizenship would not eliminate espionage, but it would remove one significant structural vulnerability and send an unambiguous signal about where American citizens' loyalties must lie.

The Degradation of Civic Meaning

Beyond the practical problems of divided loyalty, the tolerance of dual citizenship contributes to a broader degradation of what citizenship means. If American citizenship can be held simultaneously with citizenship in any number of other nations, it is reduced from a singular commitment to a mere legal status—a passport of convenience rather than a badge of belonging. This cheapening of citizenship occurs at precisely the moment when American civic life most desperately needs reinvigoration.

The United States faces a crisis of civic cohesion. Trust in institutions is at historic lows. Political polarization has reached levels not seen since the Civil War era. Voter participation, while occasionally spiking in high-profile elections, remains anemic by the standards of peer democracies. Community organizations, religious institutions, and civic associations—the intermediary structures that Tocqueville identified as the lifeblood of American democracy—continue their decades-long decline. In this environment, the signal sent by tolerating dual citizenship is exactly wrong. It tells citizens that their commitment to the American political community need not be exclusive, that the United States is merely one option among many, and that the bonds of shared citizenship are transactional rather than transcendent.

A robust democracy requires that its citizens feel a deep, primary identification with their political community. This does not mean that citizens cannot appreciate other cultures, maintain personal connections abroad, or feel affection for ancestral homelands. These are natural and often admirable sentiments. But there is a categorical difference between cultural affinity and political allegiance. One can love Italian food, speak fluent Japanese, and cherish memories of a grandmother's village in Guatemala while maintaining an exclusive political commitment to the United States. Dual citizenship collapses this distinction, transforming what should be a matter of cultural appreciation into a competing political loyalty.

The degradation of civic meaning has particularly harmful consequences for the naturalization process. The Oath of Allegiance, recited by every naturalizing citizen, contains perhaps the most solemn words in American civic life: "I hereby declare, on oath, that I absolutely and entirely renounce and abjure all allegiance and fidelity to any foreign prince, potentate, state, or sovereignty of whom or which I have heretofore been a subject or citizen." These words are magnificent in their clarity and totality. Yet under current practice, they are rendered meaningless. A naturalizing citizen speaks these words, and then walks out of the ceremony still holding a foreign passport, still voting in foreign elections, still subject to the legal obligations of a foreign sovereign. The oath becomes a performative ritual drained of substance—a lie sanctioned by the state. This hollowing out of the naturalization oath is not merely a technical inconsistency; it is a moral scandal that disrespects both the oath itself and the millions of immigrants who have taken it in genuine good faith throughout American history.

The Fairness Argument

Proponents of dual citizenship often frame the issue in terms of individual rights and personal freedom. But this framing ignores the fundamental asymmetry that dual citizenship creates among American citizens. A dual citizen enjoys advantages unavailable to their fellow Americans who hold only United States citizenship. They can live and work freely in another country without immigration restrictions. They may have access to foreign healthcare systems, educational institutions, and social safety nets funded by another nation's taxpayers. They can own property in countries that restrict foreign ownership. They can vote in foreign elections, influencing the governance of nations to which single-citizenship Americans have no comparable access. In essence, dual citizens enjoy a kind of geopolitical arbitrage—maintaining multiple options and fallback positions while their single-citizenship compatriots bear the full, undiluted consequences of American political life.

This asymmetry is particularly troubling in the context of taxation. The United States is one of very few nations that taxes its citizens on worldwide income regardless of residence. A dual citizen who relocates to their other country of citizenship may continue to owe American taxes while also owing taxes to their country of residence—but they also have the option, unavailable to non-dual citizens, of eventually renouncing American citizenship if the tax burden becomes inconvenient. Renunciation of citizenship for tax purposes has become a well-documented phenomenon, with record numbers of Americans giving up their passports in recent years. The availability of a second citizenship transforms American citizenship from an irrevocable commitment into a revocable option, exercised or abandoned according to individual financial calculation. This is not the behavior of citizens in any meaningful sense of the word; it is the behavior of consumers optimizing their portfolio of national affiliations.

Furthermore, the availability of dual citizenship creates perverse incentives in the immigration system. Birth tourism—the practice of traveling to the United States specifically to give birth on American soil, thereby securing citizenship for the child through the Fourteenth Amendment—is driven in significant part by the knowledge that the child can enjoy the benefits of American citizenship while being raised entirely abroad and maintaining primary allegiance to another nation. The child accumulates an American passport as an insurance policy, a backup plan, a hedge against political or economic instability in the country where they actually live. Whatever one's views on birthright citizenship itself, the exploitation of this provision through the mechanism of dual citizenship represents a perversion of the principle that citizenship reflects genuine membership in a political community.

The International Perspective

Those who defend dual citizenship often characterize opposition to it as parochial or nationalist, suggesting that in an increasingly interconnected world, insisting on singular allegiance is an anachronism. But this characterization ignores the fact that many of the world's most successful and admired democracies either prohibit or severely restrict dual citizenship. Japan, one of the world's most technologically advanced and internationally engaged nations, requires citizens to choose a single nationality by age twenty-two. Austria, the Netherlands, and Germany all impose significant restrictions on dual citizenship, reflecting the judgment of these mature democracies that national cohesion requires undivided political commitment. China, India, and Indonesia—nations representing billions of the world's people—do not permit dual citizenship at all. The United States, in tolerating dual citizenship without meaningful restriction, is not leading the world toward a more enlightened future; it is an outlier whose permissiveness reflects not principle but neglect.

The argument that globalization makes dual citizenship necessary or inevitable also misunderstands the nature of globalization itself. The free movement of goods, capital, ideas, and even people across borders does not require or imply the dissolution of distinct political communities. One can be a global citizen in the metaphorical sense—engaged with the world, open to other cultures, committed to international cooperation—while maintaining an exclusive political allegiance to a single nation. Indeed, the nation-state remains the fundamental unit of democratic accountability, and it is precisely through strong, cohesive national democracies that international cooperation is most effectively achieved. Weakening the bonds of national citizenship does not strengthen the international order; it undermines the very building blocks upon which that order rests.

Addressing Counterarguments

The most emotionally compelling argument against banning dual citizenship concerns the millions of Americans who currently hold dual status, many of whom acquired it involuntarily through birth. Critics argue that forcing these individuals to choose would be cruel, disruptive, and potentially unconstitutional. These concerns deserve serious engagement, but they are ultimately answerable.

First, any ban on dual citizenship would need to be implemented with reasonable transition periods, allowing affected individuals time to make informed decisions about their national allegiance. A five-to-ten-year transition period would provide ample time for dual citizens to settle their affairs, make their choice, and, if they choose to retain American citizenship, take the necessary steps to formally renounce their foreign nationality. This is not cruelty; it is the reasonable expectation that citizens make a clear commitment to their political community.

Second, the constitutional objection, rooted in Afroyim v. Rusk, is not as insurmountable as it may appear. Afroyim held that the government cannot involuntarily strip citizenship from an unwilling citizen. But a dual citizenship ban would not strip anyone of American citizenship against their will. It would present dual citizens with a choice: retain your American citizenship and renounce your foreign nationality, or retain your foreign nationality and voluntarily relinquish your American citizenship. The choice is the citizen's to make. What the government would no longer do is permit the indefinite maintenance of a contradictory status that undermines the meaning of American citizenship for everyone.

Third, critics argue that many foreign nations do not provide mechanisms for renouncing citizenship, potentially trapping dual citizens in an impossible situation. This is a legitimate practical concern, but it is addressable through diplomatic negotiation and reasonable exceptions. The United States, as the world's preeminent power, has enormous diplomatic leverage to secure agreements with other nations facilitating the renunciation process. For the rare cases in which a foreign nation truly refuses to accept renunciation, narrowly tailored exceptions could be crafted without undermining the general principle.

Finally, some argue that dual citizenship benefits the United States by creating networks of culturally connected individuals who can serve as bridges between nations, facilitating trade, diplomacy, and cultural exchange. This argument confuses cultural connection with political allegiance. An American citizen of Mexican heritage who speaks Spanish, visits family in Guadalajara, and has deep knowledge of Mexican culture is a tremendous asset to the United States—and none of these attributes require Mexican citizenship. Similarly, an American business executive operating in Germany does not need German citizenship to do business there; work permits and residency visas serve this function perfectly well. The "bridge-building" argument for dual citizenship conflates the desirability of international engagement with the necessity of divided political loyalty, a conflation that does not withstand scrutiny.

The Deeper Principle

At its core, the case for banning dual citizenship rests on a conviction about the nature of political community that transcends practical considerations of security, fairness, and civic cohesion, important as these are. The conviction is this: self-government is a serious business that demands serious commitment. The American experiment in democratic self-governance is premised on the idea that free citizens, bound together by shared allegiance and mutual obligation, can govern themselves more wisely and more justly than any external authority. This experiment has never been easy, and it has never been guaranteed to succeed. It requires that citizens invest themselves fully in the common project—that they show up not only for the benefits but for the burdens, not only for the rights but for the responsibilities, not only for the privileges but for the sacrifices.

Dual citizenship is fundamentally incompatible with this vision. It tells citizens that they need not invest themselves fully, that they can maintain a foot in another camp, that their commitment to the American experiment is conditional and reversible. It creates a class of citizens whose ultimate loyalty is permanently ambiguous—not because of any fault in their character, but because the legal structure of their citizenship makes ambiguity inevitable. And it sends a message to the world that American citizenship is not a singular commitment worthy of exclusive devotion, but merely one of several flags of convenience available to the globally mobile.

The United States has always asked much of its citizens, and in return, it has offered much. It has asked for loyalty and offered liberty. It has asked for service and offered opportunity. It has asked for allegiance and offered belonging. This reciprocal relationship—this covenant—is the beating heart of the American idea. To preserve it, we must insist that those who claim the title of American citizen do so without reservation, without qualification, and without divided loyalty. One nation, indivisible, requires nothing less than one allegiance, undivided. It is time to make that principle not merely aspirational but enforceable, by bringing the anomaly of dual citizenship to a definitive end.

When you swear the Oath of Allegiance to the United States, you speak these words: "I absolutely and entirely renounce and abjure all allegiance and fidelity to any foreign prince, potentate, state, or sovereignty."

Those are not decorative words. They are not poetry. They are a promise. And yet the moment that oath is spoken, we turn around and say, "But of course, keep your other citizenship too." We ask new Americans to renounce — and then we don't mean it.

What message does that send? That our oaths are hollow? That American citizenship is something you can hold casually, like a membership card you keep in your wallet alongside another?

I say that diminishes every single one of us.

Undivided Loyalty Is Not a Radical Idea

Let me be clear about what I am not saying. I am not questioning anyone's love of their heritage. I am not asking anyone to forget where they came from. Culture, language, family bonds, memory — these are beautiful things, and America has always been enriched by the traditions people bring to our shores.

But political allegiance is something different. Political allegiance means: When the interests of this nation and the interests of that nation collide — and they will — where do you stand?

It means: Who do you vote for? Whose military do you serve? Whose laws command your ultimate obedience? Whose tax obligations do you honor fully? Whose secrets do you keep?

These are not abstract questions. They are real, practical, and consequential.

A citizen who holds dual nationality may be called to vote in two countries — potentially shaping the politics of a foreign nation while shaping ours. They may hold office abroad. They may be subject to foreign military conscription. They may face impossible conflicts of interest in business, in government service, in matters of national security.

And we just... look the other way.

The Founders Understood This

The generation that built America was consumed with the question of loyalty — and rightly so. They had just fought a war against an empire that demanded their submission. They understood that a republic cannot survive if its citizens' commitments are fractured, conditional, or divided.

Alexander Hamilton — himself an immigrant — wrote extensively about the dangers of foreign influence and divided attachment. The Framers placed the natural-born citizen requirement on the presidency precisely because they understood that the highest office demands the most undivided allegiance.

Were they wrong? Or have we simply grown too comfortable to remember why they were right?

This Is About Equality Among Citizens

Here is something that bothers me deeply about the current system: it creates two classes of citizenship.

A natural-born American who holds only U.S. citizenship has one country, one allegiance, one political identity. They're all in. If America fails, they have nowhere else to go. Their commitment is total — not because of some legal requirement, but because of reality.

But a dual citizen has an escape hatch. They have a second passport, a second home, a second option. If things get difficult here — economically, politically, socially — they have somewhere else to turn.

That is not equal citizenship. That is citizenship with an insurance policy. And every American who doesn't have that option should ask themselves: Is that fair? Is that the same level of commitment?

When we ask young Americans to serve in our military, to pay their taxes, to sit on juries, to invest their entire futures in this country — do we not owe them fellow citizens who are equally and fully committed?

The National Security Dimension

I would be remiss if I did not address the security implications — not with fear-mongering, but with honesty.

Dual citizens serve in our government. They hold security clearances. They work in sensitive positions in defense, intelligence, diplomacy, and law enforcement. And every single one of them represents a potential — I stress potential — vector for divided loyalty, for foreign pressure, for conflicts of interest that need not exist.

Our adversaries are sophisticated. They understand the leverage that dual nationality provides. They understand that a citizen who has family abroad, property abroad, legal obligations abroad, can be pressured in ways that a solely American citizen cannot.

Why would we voluntarily maintain that vulnerability? Not out of suspicion toward any individual, but out of simple, clear-eyed prudence?

What I Propose

I propose that we restore meaning to American citizenship by adopting a clear, fair, and prospective policy:

First, that anyone seeking to naturalize as an American citizen must genuinely renounce all other citizenships — and that we verify and enforce that renunciation, as we once did, rather than treating the oath as a formality.

Second, that American citizens who voluntarily acquire citizenship in another nation be understood to have made a choice — and that choice has consequences. We should establish a reasonable transition period during which they must elect one citizenship or the other.

Third, that we provide generous timelines and compassionate processes. Nobody should be surprised. Nobody should be rushed. But everyone should eventually be asked to answer the question: Are you an American, fully and completely, or not?

Fourth, that we recognize limited, specific exceptions — perhaps for minor children of international marriages — while maintaining the clear principle that adult citizens of this republic owe it their complete political allegiance.

Answering the Objections

Now, I know the objections. I've heard them all. Let me address them honestly.

"This is nativist." No. This has nothing to do with where anyone was born, what language they speak, what color their skin is, or what God they pray to. This is about political commitment, and it applies equally to a dual American-Canadian from Toronto and a dual American-British citizen from London. This is the most egalitarian possible standard: one citizenship, one allegiance, for everyone.

"Other countries allow it." Other countries do many things we do not. America has always charted its own course. And frankly, many nations that permit dual citizenship do so out of administrative convenience, not principle. We should be guided by principle.

"It's impractical." It was practical for most of American history. It is practical in countries that enforce single citizenship today. What is truly impractical is maintaining a system that asks people to swear oaths we don't enforce and make commitments we don't expect them to honor.

"People will lose rights." People will be asked to make a choice. That is not losing a right. That is exercising one. The right to choose — fully, freely, and meaningfully — to be an American.

The Deeper Truth

At the bottom of all of this is a question about what kind of nation we want to be.

Do we want to be a country where citizenship is a profound bond — where every citizen knows that every other citizen has made the same complete commitment they have? Where we are truly, as Lincoln said, bound together by mystic chords of memory and by the choice to be one people?

Or do we want to be a country where citizenship is a transaction? A portfolio to be diversified? A convenience to be held lightly and set aside when it becomes burdensome?

I know which America I believe in. I believe in an America where citizenship means something. Where the oath is sacred. Where when you say "I am an American," you mean it with your whole heart, because you have chosen this country above all others — not out of contempt for any other nation, but out of love for this one.

E pluribus unum. Out of many, one.

Not one of two. Not one among several. One.

That is what I am asking us to restore. Not with anger. Not with suspicion. But with a clear-eyed recognition that the most valuable things in life — marriage, faith, citizenship — demand that we choose. And that the choosing is what makes them sacred.

Let us have the courage to ask that choice of every American. And let us have the courage to make it ourselves.

Thank you, and God bless the United States of America.
